DIGITAL NOMADS - Post-Pandemic Worklife

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Across the world, the combination of Covid-19 and an explosion in the use of communications technology has forever changed the way we work. Reports by McKinsey and Boston Consulting Group (which included SA in their research) indicate working from home will become a fixture of our lives. 43% of the UK’s biggest companies are adopting a hybrid model where staff will work from home two to three days a week.

On May 18th the University of Pretoria is hosting the Nobel Prize Dialogues webinar where several Nobel laureates, including Joseph Stiglitz and Mohammad Yunus will discuss the future of work, an indication that this is phenomenon is attracting the attention of some of world’s brightest minds.

COVID‑19 will be forever remembered as the virus that turned their homes into office spaces. It is also affecting people’s choices of where to live. Because going to the office is no longer required for many categories of worker, people are re-locating to environments which offer attractive lifestyles and better infrastructure and services. This is especially evident in the tech sector.


Further information:
Cape Town is home to 450 tech firms employing 40 000 people and has been ranked one of the world’s fastest-growing regions for foreign direct investment, according to a report from fDi Intelligence, a data division of the Financial Times group. So it’s no wonder the world’s biggest online retailer, Amazon, is to establish its new Africa headquarters in River Club, Cape Town, in a mixed use R4 billion development. Amazon’s decision could be the latest in an emerging trend that sees Cape Town as the leading “tech” city in Africa and preferred home to tech workers, a trend that the Covid-19 pandemic has accelerated.
 
After being voted one of the “Best Places For Remote Working in 2021” and receiving a Safe Travel Stamp from the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC), Cape Town is looking to position itself as an ideal “workation” destination in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic.
 
Mayoral Committee Member for Economic Opportunities in the City of Cape Town is proposing a remote-working visa to attract “digital nomads”. “We are seeing innovation within the tourism sector to accommodate the changed behaviour of remote working by offering affordable long-term stays, including other benefits required to work remotely and we will expand this message through the broad range of products and businesses who can use a leg up in this challenging time,” says Vos.

The Remote Work Visa, highlighted by Vos as the next logical step for government’s eVisa programme, would allow visitors from more than 100 countries to complete their applications online, thereby avoiding the need to appear at embassies or consulates in-person.

How does that impact office and retail space? South Africa now has in the region 2.4 million square metres of empty office space available, - no wonder the growing trend to convert unused office space for residential use.

Offices and retail being re-purposed into accommodation, leisure and activity centres. For example Africrest Properties are converting 30 000 sq m of PWC offices in Sunninghill into 700 residential units. All around Sandton and Rosebank office space is lying empty, radical deals are being offered like first three months free.

This also brought a property boom to places like Plettenberg Bay, Mossel Bay and Karoo towns which are the beneficiaries of “semigration” for people who are realizing they can work from wherever they want to live.

Working from home doesn’t suit everyone. Local research shows 40% of South Africans feel the pandemic has had a negative impact on their working life and career. Estelle Meiring, a director at Paragon Architects says the need for human interaction will keep the office alive albeit in a different setting than we know now and the emphasis of office space will shift away from “ a place to sit and work to a place to communicate, collaborate and build company culture.”

Hot desk/office sharing is another growing trend, evidenced by Workshop 17 and The Link in Rosebank, Johannesburg – people/businesses no longer need large permanent premises but can share office space and resources more efficiently

With remote working poised to be more common post-pandemic, almost two-thirds (63%) of surveyed respondents support remote work policies being regulated by the South African government.

This is one of the key findings of research commissioned by software company Citrix and conducted by research firm OnePoll.

The research is based on a survey of 4 250 office-based workers in the UK, France, Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, including 500 South African respondents, between 2 February and 15 February.
The survey notes that post-pandemic, half (52%) of respondents favour a hybrid model where they can work from both the office and remotely, with just 17% wanting to go back to an office every day.
Where South African companies did not offer remote work prior to the pandemic, it was usually because they feared their employees would not work the same number of hours as in the office. But the research shows three-quarters (76%) of respondents work at least the same number of hours, with 53% working longer hours than from the office.

Press Release:


L I F E S T Y L E



The Future of Work

Across the world, COVID-19 lockdowns coincided with an explosion in the use of versatile digital communications technology, as people were forced to work from home. Some trend analysts now say remote work will become the norm and forever change the workplace. City centres globally are suffering from the so-called office wasteland effect with millions of square metres of office space standing empty – and South Africa is no different with the country now having the largest vacancy rates in history. What will become of the millions of empty square metres of office space? Voted one of the Best Places For Remote Working in 2021, Cape Town is positioning itself as the ideal workstation destination in the post-pandemic world of work – could this revive the tourism industry? Carte Blanche encounters out-of-the-box thinking that’s bringing life back to dying spaces as we examine the life of the new post-pandemic digital nomad.

Producer: Diana Lucas | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


Francois: Just imagine 2 years ago walking into a boardroom and coming up with this great suggestion that everyone should go home and start working from home you would be thrown out of the boardroom.

V/O
For Property economist, Prof Francois Viruly, COVID has renergised the propery space.

Francois: It has opened up a world we weren’t seeing, possibilities that we weren’t considering.

Link: Johannesburg, Cape Town…city centres around the world are suffering from the office wasteland effect. In South Africa there are around 2,4 million square metres are just lying empty –
… So what to do with all this empty space? Well some developers are thinking out of the box and those empty offices are being transformed into cosy work-from-home apartments like this, 1000’s of them.


“As you can see demolition has just started.

V/O
Grant Friedman showed us around.

Grant Friedman
Director, Africrest Properties

Grant: These offices were built to be offices they weren’t designed and specified to become an apartment building so it takes quiet a lot of work to retrofit them.
Derek: So this office space will hopefully be one apartment

V/O
And Hotel SKY in Cape Town, previously 27 floors of offices, it’s now transformed to a Las Vegas look alike.

Francois: One of the big words in the property market is the re purposing of office space we have a space used for an office can we use it for something else and more and more property companies are going to look very much like hotel groups.
Grant:.. We’ve created work from home environments space we offer Gyms for our tenants work from home facilities we like to imagine it as a hotel you…hotel you can live in forever.
V/O
A digital marketing specialist, Alexia Pienaar works for a Canadian company. It took the pandemic for her career to go global.

Alexia Pienaar
Digital Marketing Specialist

Alexia: I think I spent about 8 months looked during work and nothing came about and so I had to start going outside of SA
Derek: So while SA has closed down in some way the digital space has opened up?
Alexia: I didn’t understand how powerful the digital space would be and achieve these projects that we are ding I thought that you would need that face to face and being around customers actually you don’t you don’t.

Alexia :I have never seen my boss looks like, in my first interview I put my camera on I dressed up, make up on, my hair and then I had the screen on and all of a sudden there was no picture on my end so I was like oh would you like my camera on…No No its fine don’t worry and then we start a 3 hour interview process and then to this day I still don’t know what he looks like.

Link 4 20 – 4 30
Remote working and the future of work are hot topics, from dinner table conversations to business magazines and property economists.

Francois - Lets not underestimate the digital divide in South Africa We don’t all have the same access to the internet easy with a smart phone in your pocket very different when you are in rural Limpopo. So for cities it will be interesting there are cities instead of roads use for free wi fi because I spend more time on the internet highway than on the concrete highway.

V/O
Cape Town was recently voted one of the world’s 50 best destinations for remote workers James Vos, who heads up economic opportunities and tourism for the City, is proposing a remote working visa to attract Digital Nomads.

Alderman James Vos
City of Cape Town
MMC Economic Opportunities & Tourism

Derek: Persuade government to issue work from home visas
James Vos: Our proposal is amendment be made to Section 11 of the immigration act which relates to an extension of visa beyond 90 days.
Derek: Overseas company not taking jobs form locals
That’s indeed case so you must present sufficient financial resources, you also need to provide evidence of employment abroad as well as sufficient income from employment.

Guillaume: Tell you what life is a beach….

V/O
Guillaume de Smedt is one of Cape Town’s 40 000 tech workers and no he’s not actually on the beach….but the beauty of remote working is you can be anywhere. While the world might be a digital nomad’s oyster they are now competing in an international field

Guillaume de Smedt
Bevy: Product Manager

Guillaume: Competition is much tougher, Its really hard its not easy you still have to do the work, and if you are not the best person they can go to somebody else because they can get anybody anywhere in the world so you have to up your game.

V/O
And cities are competing to attract these nomads.

Derek: James when it comes to attracting those digital nomads where to you see your competition coming from?
James: If you think about the tech sector our biggest competition in Africa is Lagos. Globally Norway Australia, Portugal and Dubai already implemented these visas so competition is out there. The world has been turned upside down Covid 19 brought about such drastic shifts that require us to significantly re consider the ways we work and live and that includes the tourism sector which employs nearly 300 000 people in Cape Town.
Derek : So slaap stad no more
James No more no more.

V/O
Sandras Phiri founded Start up Circles to bring together investors and entrepreneurs across Africa. In February last year he was in Silicon Valley and returned to launch his business. Then Covid hits and everything changes.

Sandras Phiri
Founder: Startup Circles

Sandras: So we had to pivot and go completely digital.

V/O
Sandras and his wife Lelemba had to immediately transform the way they operated… ( Up Sound on Zoom with his wife) The result is their entrepreneurs and investors now come from all over the world.

Sandras: So we have our main investor investing in 10 companies during lock down maybe before would have needed meetings in person and the process would have been longer but now investors are investing without having to meet people face to face. We we were in Kruger and we were doing a demo day So we were with entrepreneurs across the continent and Europe and I was sitting in Kruger.

Alexia: You’re always connected I will get a message from my boss its 3 o clock my time and then you quickly jump on line to make sure you have done everything.

Guillaume: Time zones are not very nice to handle My current lifestyle is to wake up in the morning my wife and I will surf midday my official hours are 2 to midnight so I starts working supper break kid down

V/O
A few months into lockdown corporate bosses were keen for their staff to work from home to reduce Covid infections. But things have changed - 43% of the UK’s biggest companies are adopting a hybrid model where staff will work from home two to three days a week.

Sandras : The future of work is going to be hybrid which I think is a good thing because a lot of time there are a lot of trips that were completely unnecessary a lot of meetings just wasting time..

Francois: …As society we didn’t get the luxury of time maybe we will move back a bit but I doubt completely back I don’t think we should.

Estelle Meiring, a director at Paragon Architects says the need for human interaction will keep the office alive albeit in a different setting than we know now and the emphasis of office space will shift away from “ a place to sit and work to a place to communicate, collaborate and build company culture.” Hot desk/office sharing is another growing trend, evidenced by Workshop 17 and The Link in Rosebank, Johannesburg – people/businesses no longer need large permanent premises but can share office space and resources more efficiently With remote working poised to be more common post-pandemic, almost two-thirds (63%) of surveyed respondents support remote work policies being regulated by the South African government. This is one of the key findings of research commissioned by software company Citrix and conducted by research firm OnePoll. The research is based on a survey of 4 250 office-based workers in the UK, France, Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands, including 500 South African respondents, between 2 February and 15 February. The survey notes that post-pandemic, half (52%) of respondents favour a hybrid model where they can work from both the office and remotely, with just 17% wanting to go back to an office every day. Where South African companies did not offer remote work prior to the pandemic, it was usually because they feared their employees would not work the same number of hours as in the office. But the research shows three-quarters (76%) of respondents work at least the same number of hours, with 53% working longer hours than from the office.
